title: Interest
objective: After this level you can explain interest as the price of borrowing money.
summary: Interest is the price of borrowing, usually a yearly rate. Lenders charge for waiting and for risk. Hammurabi's laws set interest rates over 1,000 years before coins.

cards.headline: Interest is older than coins.
cards.body: Mesopotamian laws, including Hammurabi's code, were setting interest rates in the 18th century BCE. Lydia's first coins from Level 4 came more than 1,000 years later, around 650 BCE. People have been paying to borrow for a very long time.

cards.headline: Rent for money
cards.body: Interest is the price of borrowing: the fee a borrower pays a lender for the use of money. It's usually quoted as a rate. Borrow $100 at 5% a year, and a year's use of that money costs you $5. Think of it as rent. You get to use someone else's money for a while, and like a rented flat, it goes back at the end, with the rent on top.

cards.headline: Why lenders charge
cards.body: Lending means waiting. If someone would pay $95 today for a promise of $100 in a year, the $5 difference is interest, the reward for giving up money now. Risk raises the price too. Mesopotamian law allowed 20% on loans of silver but more on barley, because barley loans usually went to the poor and were seen as riskier.

cards.context: When you borrow, you pay it. When you deposit money in certain accounts, the bank may pay you. Level 21's spread lives in the gap between those two rates: the bank charges borrowers more than it pays savers.

cards.headline: Interest: priced
learned: Interest is the price of borrowing money
It is usually quoted as a yearly rate
Lenders charge for waiting and for risk
Hammurabi's laws set rates before coins existed

options.label: A tax charged on every bank deposit
options.rationale: It isn't a tax: it's a lender's fee for the use of money.

options.label: The fee for swapping one currency for another
options.rationale: That was the money changers' exchange trade.

options.label: The price paid for the use of borrowed money
A bank's share of every salary it handles
options.rationale: Banks earn on lending, not by taking a cut of pay.

questions.explanation: Interest is the price, or fee, a borrower pays a lender for the use of money.

questions.prompt: Why did Mesopotamian law allow a higher interest rate on barley loans than on silver?

options.label: Barley loans usually went to the poor and were seen as riskier
Barley was worth more than silver
options.rationale: The rate reflected risk, not the value of barley.

options.label: The king owned all the barley
options.rationale: The reason was risk: barley loans usually went to the poor.

questions.explanation: More risk, higher price: barley loans usually went to poorer borrowers and were seen as riskier.

questions.prompt: Which came first: laws setting interest rates, or the Lydian coins from Level 4?

options.label: The coins, by about a century
options.rationale: Hammurabi's laws came first, by over a thousand years.

options.label: Both appeared in the same century
options.rationale: They were more than a thousand years apart.

options.label: Interest laws only began with medieval banks
options.rationale: Hammurabi's code set rates in the 18th century BCE.

options.label: Interest laws, by more than 1,000 years

questions.explanation: Hammurabi's code (18th century BCE) set interest rates more than 1,000 years before Lydia's coins (around 650 BCE).
